story: Silvan Urfer was first author of the Atlas study URF2017 in GeroScience. It was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 24 healthy middle-aged pet dogs. They got low-dose rapamycin or placebo for 10 weeks. The treated dogs had no clinical side effects, and heart ultrasound suggested better heart function. The trial was small and short, so it only supports testing in larger groups. PubMed lists Urfer at the University of Washington and the Dog Aging Project in Seattle.

highlights.URF2017: First author: reported that 10 weeks of low-dose rapamycin caused no clinical side effects in pet dogs and may have improved heart function.

story: Xiaoli Cui is first author of a 2026 study in the Journal of Ethnopharmacology. In mice with kidney damage from high blood pressure (caused by angiotensin II), the plant compound forsythoside A bound a protein called ASCL1 and blocked a downstream CCNB1/mTOR axis. That increased mitophagy, the removal of damaged mitochondria, and reduced ferroptosis, a form of cell death. The protection did not come from lowering blood pressure. PubMed lists her at the College of Pharmacy, Beihua University.

The usual rise of about 40% in muscle protein synthesis in the first one to two hours was blocked. The study measured short-term protein synthesis, not muscle growth. story: Nao Hosokawa is first author of an Atlas study (HOS2009) in cultured cells on how mTORC1 holds back autophagy, the cell's recycling process. The group found that Atg13 forms a large complex with ULK1 and FIP200, and that mTORC1 joins this complex when nutrients are plentiful and phosphorylates ULK1 and Atg13. Starvation or rapamycin releases that brake and autophagy can begin. PubMed lists Hosokawa at Tokyo Medical and Dental University.

current.lab_name: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center (San Antonio, Texas, USA)
current.role: First author of a 2010 study in Alzheimer's disease model mice linking mTOR, amyloid-beta and Tau.

story: Antonella Caccamo was first author of a 2010 mouse study from the Department of Physiology at the University of Texas Health Science Center in San Antonio. It asked how mTOR, amyloid-beta and Tau fit together in Alzheimer's disease.

The work found a loop. Amyloid-beta raises mTOR activity, and high mTOR blocks autophagy, the cell's clean-up process, so amyloid and Tau build up further. In a mouse model of the disease, rapamycin broke the loop, improved memory and lowered both amyloid and Tau. Blocking autophagy removed the amyloid benefit. This was done in mice, not in people. Caccamo also appears in a 2012 Atlas paper, but PubMed gives no affiliation for that record, so it is not covered here.

highlights.CAC2010: First author of the mouse study showing that rapamycin rescued memory and lowered amyloid-beta and Tau through autophagy.

pubmed_affiliation: Department of Physiology, University of Texas Health Science Center, San Antonio, Texas 78245, USA.

studies.title: Molecular interplay between mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR), amyloid-beta, and Tau: effects on cognitive impairments.
studies.finding: Revealed a vicious cycle: amyloid-beta RAISES mTOR activity, and high mTOR in turn blocks the autophagy needed to clear amyloid and tau - so the disease feeds itself. Rapamycin broke the loop in 3xTg-AD mice, rescuing memory and lowering BOTH amyloid and tau, with autophagy induction shown to be necessary for the reduction in amyloid levels.

studies.title: Tsc tumour suppressor proteins antagonize amino-acid-TOR signalling
studies.finding:
The authors asked how the Tsc1 and Tsc2 tumour suppressors relate to TOR, the nutrient-sensing kinase. They showed that Tsc1 and Tsc2 can physically associate with TOR and act upstream of TOR in fly genetic tests. In fly and mammalian cells lacking Tsc1 or Tsc2, S6K activity rose, and this increase depended on TOR. S6K normally switches off when cells are starved of amino acids, but cells without Tsc1-Tsc2 stayed resistant to that starvation. The authors proposed that the Tsc1-Tsc2 complex restrains the TOR response to amino acids.

PubMed lists her at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

story: BAS2012 (2012) is BOLERO-2, a phase 3 randomised trial in 724 women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. Adding everolimus to exemestane roughly doubled progression-free survival (10.6 versus 4.1 months by central review). Michael Gnant is a middle author in the author list. PIC2014 (2014) is the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2. Median overall survival was 31.0 months with everolimus plus exemestane and 26.6 months with placebo plus exemestane, a difference that was not statistically significant. Michael Gnant is a middle author in the author list.

PubMed gives no affiliation for this author in the BOLERO-2 primary report. The affiliation here comes from the final overall-survival report, which lists the same author by surname and initials and shares many co-authors with the primary report.

story: Bo Tang was first author of the Atlas study TAN2026, which looked at clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a kidney cancer. ZMYND8 can then work with ZHX2 to switch on the NEK7 gene, and p70S6K is activated by another route that does not need mTOR. A drug built to destroy NEK7 restored everolimus sensitivity. PubMed lists Tang at the Department of Urology, West China Hospital, Sichuan University.

studies.title: SPOP-mediated ZMYND8 ubiquitination and phase separation exclusion drives mTOR inhibitor resistance in kidney cancer
studies.finding: Identifies a mechanism of mTOR-inhibitor (everolimus/temsirolimus) resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma: SPOP-driven K63-linked ubiquitination of ZMYND8 excludes it from phase-separation compartments, enabling a ZMYND8-ZHX2 complex that drives NEK7 transcription and alternative p70S6K activation independent of mTOR inhibition. A NEK7-targeting PROTAC restored everolimus sensitivity in ccRCC cells and mouse tumors, nominating NEK7 as a target to overcome mTOR-inhibitor resistance.

story: Zhi-Lie Cao was first author of a 2026 review article in Frontiers in Oncology. PubMed lists the author in the Department of Urology at Taizhou Hospital of Zhejiang Province, which is affiliated with Wenzhou Medical University, and also at a hospital in Hangzhou.

The review looks at Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome, a genetic condition caused by loss of the FLCN gene. It argues that the old picture of mTORC1 simply being switched on everywhere does not fit. FLCN acts on RagC/D, so mTORC1 control is selective. Losing both gene copies drives kidney tumours, while having only one working copy is enough to cause lung and skin problems. Being a review, it reports no new experiments.

studies.title: Substrate-selective mTORC1 regulation and gene dosage-dependent tissue divergence in Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome
studies.finding: Reframes Birt-Hogg-Dube (BHD) syndrome beyond the classic 'global mTORC1 hyperactivation' model: FLCN acts as a GAP for RagC/D, giving substrate-selective (not global) mTORC1 control. Biallelic FLCN loss drives kidney tumors via MiT/TFE nuclear accumulation, while haploinsufficiency alone is sufficient for lung and skin lesions -- resolving the 'mTORC1 paradox' via gene dosage and signaling timing. Narrative synthesis of human genetics and mouse mechanistic data.
